'''Etchemin''' was a language of the [[Algonquian languages|Algonquian]] language family, spoken in early colonial times on the coast of [[Maine]]. The word ''Etchemin'' is thought to be either [[French language|French]] alteration of an Algonquian word for 'canoe' or a translation of ''Skidijn'', the native word for people in use by the inhabitants of the [[St. John River|St. John]] and [[Saint Croix Island, Maine|St. Croix]] Rivers.

The only known record of the Etchemin language is a list of the numbers from one to ten recorded by [[Marc Lescarbot]] in the early 17th century and published in his book ''The History of New France'' (1609).<ref>{{Cite book |last=Lescarbot |first=Marc |url=http://archive.org/details/historyofnewfran01lesc |title=The history of New France |last2=Biggar |first2=Henry Percival |last3=Grant |first3=W. L. (William Lawson) |last4=Ganong |first4=William F. (William Francis) |last5=Champlain Society |date=1907 |publisher=Toronto : Champlain Society |others=Robarts - University of Toronto}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Lescarbot |first=Marc |url=http://archive.org/details/histoiredelanouv00lesc_3 |title=Histoire de la Nouvelle France : contenant les navigations, découvertes, & habitations faites par les François és Indes Occidentes & Nouvelle-France souz l'avoeu & authorité de noz rois tres-chrétiens, & les diverses fortunes d'iceux en l'execution de ces choses, depuis cent ans jusques à hui. En quoy est comprise l'histoire morale, naturele, & geographique de la dite province: avec les tables & figures d'icelle. |date=1609 |publisher=A Paris : Chez Iean Milot, tenant sa boutique sur les degrez de la grand'salle du Palais. |others=John Carter Brown Library}}</ref> The numerals in the list match those of [[Malecite-Passamaquoddy language|Malecite-Passamaquoddy]], [[Eastern Abenaki]], as well as languages of southern New England such as [[Wampanoag language|Wampanoag]], but as a set they do not match any other [[Algonquian languages|Algonquian]] language. The Etchemin language disappeared not long after Lescarbot's visit, and it is unknown what became of the tribe. All other language records called 'Etchemin', under more detailed analysis, appear to be the neighboring [[Malecite-Passamaquoddy language]].
